title: Historical and future climate niche of Colombian glaciers: A multi-statistical analysis
content:
by Maria Paula Rivera Reyes, Adriana Sanchez, Alvaro Avila-Diaz, Jorge L. Ceballos, Benjamin Quesada

Since the mid-20th century, tropical glacier recession has accelerated, but substantial uncertainty remains regarding their disappearence timing. In Colombia, only six glacierized areas remain between 11° N and 2° N, and most of the country’s glacier cover has already disappeared. Developing novel and integrative methods for predicting glacier retreat and understanding the climatic drivers of glacier change is therefore critical for anticipating future water availability and ecosystem responses in high-mountain regions. In this study, we innovatively used the Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) model to estimate the potential distribution of glaciers in Sierra Nevada El Cocuy (the largest extent) and Santa Isabel (lowest extent) in Colombia, under multiple climate-change scenarios and time periods. We also used multilinear models to analyze in-situ glacier mass-balance records with climate data from Terra to identify the most influential climatic drivers of glacier mass loss. Our results indicate that Santa Isabel glacier and El Cocuy glacier are projected to lose up to 90% of their suitable area by 2021–2040 and 2040–2060, respectively, under high-emission scenarios. The importance of climatic variables in glacier distribution differs between sites. For Cocuy, temperature of the wettest quarter (48%) and precipitation of the driest quarter (48%) were most relevant variables, while for Santa Isabel, temperature of the driest quarter dominated (92%). In situ mass-balance records show that temperature is the dominant driver of glacier mass loss at both locations (45–65%), which is concerning given that temperature increases across Colombia are unequivocal in all climate projections. Wind, solar radiation, and precipitation further modulate glacier response in site-specific ways, with a more prominent role at El Cocuy. These findings highlight the urgent need to expand glaciological and climate monitoring and provide an integrated analytical approach with potential applicability in other mountain regions, subject to regional characteristics and data availability.
